13 Nov 2026Imperial College London; University of Antwerp and Antwerp University Hospital; Maastricht University Medical Center; Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center; Zhongshan Hospital of Fudan University

AI-enhanced electrocardiography for detection and prediction of dilated cardiomyopathy

In the journal abstract, an AI-ECG model trained on more than 330,000 ECG–echocardiogram pairs detected the dilated-cardiomyopathy phenotype (AUROC 0.87–0.97) and predicted later disease (C-index 0.80–0.87). In familial cohorts, five-year negative predictive values were 95.5% in Antwerp and 91.5% in Maastricht; positive predictive values were 42.4% and 39.4%. These are diagnostic and risk-prediction findings, not demonstrated clinical benefit.

Technology: Explainable deep learning model applied to electrocardiography

11 Nov 2026Google Research

Wearable-based health age models for cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic risk profiling and coaching

Google Research reported a wearable-based health-age model associated with subsequent hypertension, cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes in the All of Us cohort (22,748 participants). A companion world model simulated 12-week trajectories. In 490 blinded paired reviews, coaches preferred simulation-grounded plans in 71.4% of evaluations; physicians rated 97.6% of physiological claims accurate. This summary is limited to the November 11, 2026 institutional blog. The authors state all evaluations were offline and retrospective; clinical effectiveness and durable habit change require prospective trials.

Technology: Coachable health-age model, SensorWM action-conditioned world model, feasibility-constrained optimizer with a language model agent, multimodal CKM deviation model

9 Nov 2026New York University Grossman School of Medicine

PREVIA: LLM ensemble predicts PTSD risk from emergency department trauma narratives

In the journal abstract, PREVIA used trauma narratives from 145 patients at two New York City trauma centers to predict PTSD assessed one month later. Reported AUROC was 78.49% ± 5.75%, with precision 46.76% ± 8.66%. On 30 randomly selected patients, its performance was comparable to one PTSD-specialist emergency clinician. The authors describe these as initial findings requiring larger independent-cohort validation; prospective collection does not establish prospective evaluation of a locked model.

Technology: PREVIA clinically informed large language model ensemble

8 Nov 2026North Medical Center Hiroshima City Asa Citizens Hospital

Deep learning ECG model separates Takotsubo syndrome from anterior STEMI, with a randomized reader study

A preprint reports external validation of an ECG-image ensemble for Takotsubo syndrome versus anterior STEMI in 95 participants: accuracy 0.914 and AUC 0.970. Among 70 readers, estimated diagnostic correctness rose from 0.632 unaided to 0.864 with AI. Only the fourth phase randomized assistance conditions; AI-assisted reader accuracy remained below model accuracy. This summary is limited to the abstract and version 3 preprint dated November 8, 2026; the first version was posted October 19.

Technology: Self-supervised deep learning ensemble with Grad-CAM explanations

5 Nov 2026Google Research

Signs of hypertension detected by a smartwatch

Prospective study of 196 people at five US sites, compared with 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure measurement: 65.8% sensitivity and 90.0% specificity for screening, and 78.4% and 90.9% in the confirmatory test (48 participants). A feasibility study; it does not replace the cuff, and many cases are missed.

Technology: AI-PPG-ACC-HTN (photoplethysmography and accelerometer)

2 Nov 2026Nanjing Medical University, School of Public Health, Department of Epidemiology and Center for Global Health; UK Biobank

LightGBM feature selection identifies a four-protein panel associated with incident chronic kidney disease

In a prospective UK Biobank cohort of 27,429 participants without baseline chronic kidney disease, the study evaluated 2,920 plasma proteins and found 205 associated with incident CKD after protein-wide Cox regression with Bonferroni correction. LASSO reduced these to 23 candidates and LightGBM feature selection identified EDA2R, GDF15, HAVCR1 and SCARB2 as a four-protein panel. The protein panel alone had an AUC of 0.796 versus 0.805 for demographic variables; adding the proteins to the demographic model raised AUC to 0.830 in the study data.

Technology: Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) feature selection

Relevance 40 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

Result, AI contribution and limits

Evidence context (descriptions follow the cited sources; test type is a catalog classification):

  • Publication status: Peer-reviewed paper

  • Tested: In a prospective UK Biobank cohort of 27,429 participants without baseline chronic kidney disease, the study evaluated 2,920 plasma proteins and found 205 associated with incident CKD after protein-wide Cox regression with Bonferroni correction. Protein selection and prediction were assessed internally within UK Biobank; prospective cohort collection does not establish prospective evaluation of a previously locked predictor.
  • Still unknown: The abstract reports a prospective UK Biobank cohort and internal analyses; the four-protein model did not outperform the demographic model alone (AUC 0.796 vs 0.805, p=0.14), though combining the proteins with demographics improved AUC to 0.830. The authors state external validation is needed before clinical application. Protein associations and model selection do not establish causal roles or clinical utility.
  • AI role: After protein-wide Cox association screening, LASSO selected 23 candidate proteins and LightGBM-based feature selection identified four proteins for the incident-CKD prediction panel. The study assessed their predictive contribution with demographic covariates and sensitivity analyses; these algorithms selected risk markers rather than demonstrating causal protein effects.

Evidence sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42968231/

Claude's early progress in drug development

Anthropic reports early results with six partners: a CAR T-cell receptor design about 70% shorter that enabled immune cells to produce about 10 times more receptors; about 35,000 antibody designs in one month, yielding 20 candidates; and a document review that found all 11 human-identified issues plus seven more in 89% less time. The work is mostly preclinical and reported by Anthropic.

AI-designed brain-penetrant HER2 inhibitor IAM1363 shows durable responses in Phase 1/1b

Iambic reported updated results from an open-label Phase 1/1b study of its AI-designed HER2 inhibitor IAM1363. At the August 31, 2026 cutoff, 122 participants had received treatment across four study parts; the company reported antitumor and intracranial responses and that more than half of participants treated at 960 mg remained on treatment. 22 Oct 2026The First People's Hospital of Qinzhou; The First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University

Machine learning identifies SIK1 as an epilepsy driver validated in rat models

Machine-learning screening of LKB1-pathway genes in GEO data prioritized SIK1. In a PTZ-induced rat epilepsy model, SIK1 knockdown delayed seizures and shortened their duration, whereas overexpression worsened severity. The paper abstract also reports that restoring downstream NR4A2 counteracted SIK1-related effects in rescue and neuronal experiments. These are preclinical findings, not evidence of treatment efficacy in people. This summary is limited to the abstract and publication metadata.

Technology: Machine learning screening of LKB1 pathway genes on GEO dataset GSE143272

The Virtual Biotech: a multi-agent AI framework for drug development decisions

The Virtual Biotech journal abstract reports a human-guided multi-agent analysis of 55,984 trials. Drugs targeting cell-type-specific genes were associated with a 48% greater likelihood of reaching market and 32% fewer adverse events. The system also proposed a lung-cancer strategy and inferred possible reasons for a terminated ulcerative-colitis trial. These are retrospective associations and hypotheses, not demonstrated treatment benefits. The date represents the 2026-10-22 journal version; the linked preprint, including the same reported association, first appeared on 2026-02-23.

APOLLAI, a multimodal AI system, versus EMS personnel for prehospital detection of stroke-related deficits

20 Oct 2026Anthropic

Claude designs binders against five scorpion neurotoxins

In a mostly autonomous 64-hour campaign, Claude designed minibinders against five neurotoxins. External labs tested 211 designs, 17 of which met the criteria; the best (Cn2-B1 and Cn2-B2) had affinities in the low nanomolar range. Only recombinant toxins were tested, with no neutralization tests in cells or animals; Anthropic does not claim to have produced an antivenom.

Technology: Claude

Family Claude: profile · models page

Relevance 60 medicine Original source Suggest a correction

Publication: Announcement only · Test context: direct test. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

Result, AI contribution and limits

Evidence context (descriptions follow the cited sources; test type is a catalog classification):

  • Publication status: Announcement only
  • Test type: direct test
  • Tested: External labs tested 211 designs by surface plasmon resonance: Adaptyv Bio in cell-free expression and Twist Bioscience in human kidney cells; a binder needed KD of 1 µM or tighter in every replicate at both labs and no CLEC12A signal, giving 17 binders. The two collaborating external laboratories tested candidates from the discovery project; this establishes direct testing rather than a separately established independent follow-up replication.
  • Still unknown: Only recombinant toxins were tested, with no neutralization in cells or animals; the authors do not know whether the binders neutralize venom and do not claim an antivenom; multitoxin designs failed.
  • AI role: Claude selected toxin structures and hotspots, generated 318,484 designs, filtered and co-folded them, ran about 24 hours autonomously, then produced 180 selected designs after human follow-ups.

Evidence sources: https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-scorpion-toxin-binder-design

Computer-vision and metabolomics fusion links paired serum–urine flux mismatch to early diabetic kidney disease

In a two-center cohort of 364 participants with type 2 diabetes and controls, targeted serum/urine metabolite measurements found a high-serum/low-urine pattern for indoxyl sulfate and related metabolites in early diabetic kidney disease (DKD), consistent with reduced tubular secretion. Computer vision quantified urine foam stability and chromaticity; Random Forest recursive feature elimination selected these image features together with metabolite ratios and clinical variables for the FluxPro-DKD classifier. It distinguished DKD from diabetes without kidney disease with AUC 0.90 in discovery and 0.85 in a geographically distinct external cohort of 82.

Relevance 53 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

Result, AI contribution and limits

Evidence context (descriptions follow the cited sources; test type is a catalog classification):

  • Publication status: Peer-reviewed paper
  • Test type: retrospective or benchmark
  • Tested: In a two-center cohort of 364 participants with type 2 diabetes and controls, targeted serum/urine metabolite measurements found a high-serum/low-urine pattern for indoxyl sulfate and related metabolites in early diabetic kidney disease (DKD), consistent with reduced tubular secretion.

RF-RFE selected eight predictors, including digital urine features and serum-to-urine metabolite ratios, for the fusion classifier distinguishing early DKD from type 2 diabetes without DKD. The biochemical interpretation of flux mismatch as reduced tubular secretory capacity is based on measured metabolite ratios and literature-supported interpretation; transporter expression was not measured.

Prospective multicenter validation of TriVerity links a 29-mRNA host response to infection type and near-term severity

In the prospective SEPSIS-SHIELD study, a machine-learning blood test using isothermal amplification of 29 host-response mRNAs was evaluated in adults presenting to 22 emergency departments with suspected infection or sepsis. Among 1,222 patients with valid results, its bacterial and viral scores distinguished clinically adjudicated infection status with AUROCs of 0.83 and 0.91, respectively, and the system also produced a separate score for risk of ICU-level care within seven days. The test’s high/very-high and low/very-low interpretation bands had 92–99% sensitivities and specificities for selected infection/severity endpoints.

Technology: TriVerity on the Myrna instrument, using logistic-regression classifiers on expression measurements for 29 host-response mRNAs

Relevance 60 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: prospective or independent check. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

Result, AI contribution and limits

Evidence context (descriptions follow the cited sources; test type is a catalog classification):

  • Publication status: Peer-reviewed paper
  • Test type: prospective or independent check
  • Tested: In the prospective SEPSIS-SHIELD study, a machine-learning blood test using isothermal amplification of 29 host-response mRNAs was evaluated in adults presenting to 22 emergency departments with suspected infection or sepsis.
  • Still unknown: This is prospective diagnostic/prognostic validation of a specific host-response test, not discovery of a causal infection mechanism and not evidence that use of the score improves patient outcomes or antibiotic decisions. Of 1,441 enrolled patients, 1,222 had valid test results; the main diagnostic analysis used 729 consensus-adjudicated patients, and 1,120 were evaluable for prognosis. Clinical adjudication is not a perfect microbiological gold standard, and the study reports lower accuracy when uncertain adjudications are included. Performance and predictive values may vary with local infection prevalence and case mix. This is distinct from the earlier VB10 10-gene signature paper (DOI 10.1016/j.ebiom.2021.103352), which used different genes, cohorts and a different diagnostic score.
  • AI role: The locked machine-learning classifiers convert the amplified host-response mRNA profile into separate likelihood scores for bacterial infection, viral infection and need for critical-care interventions within seven days. The multicenter clinical study measured how those AI-generated scores performed against blinded physician adjudication and near-term clinical endpoints.

Evidence sources: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-025-03933-y

18 Aug 2025Huashan Hospital, Fudan University; Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University; Xiamen University; Xiang An Biomedicine Laboratory

Machine learning identifies serum protein signatures for progression from asymptomatic atherosclerosis to ischemic stroke

In a discovery cohort of 43 patients with asymptomatic large-artery atherosclerosis and a validation cohort of 39, investigators combined serum proteomics with machine learning to distinguish acute ischemic stroke from large-artery atherosclerosis. XGBoost selected a three-protein panel (RNASE4, HBA1 and ATF6B; reported AUC 0.917, specificity 80%) and a six-protein panel distinguishing patients from healthy controls (reported AUC 0.971, specificity 86%). ELISA assays confirmed higher GUCA2A and FLNA in patient groups.

Technology: XGBoost machine-learning models applied to serum proteomics; DeepPRM-Stellar targeted mass spectrometry supported peptide validation and panel optimization

14 Aug 2025Johnson & Johnson; UK Biobank; Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative collaborators

Machine learning finds plasma protein signals up to 14 years before Parkinson diagnosis

Using UK Biobank measurements of 2,937 plasma proteins, researchers found 446 dysregulated proteins in incident Parkinson cases and used machine learning to select a 23-protein panel for prediction. The panel achieved test AUCs of 0.78 in incident and 0.795 in prevalent cases; nine selected proteins were already dysregulated 10–14 years before diagnosis. In a separate Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative cohort, a 16-protein subset shared between platforms achieved validation AUC up to 0.76.

Technology: Support vector machine and other machine-learning models, with recursive feature elimination for panel selection

Relevance 53 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

Result, AI contribution and limits

Evidence context (descriptions follow the cited sources; test type is a catalog classification):

  • Publication status: Peer-reviewed paper
  • Test type: retrospective or benchmark
  • Tested: Using UK Biobank measurements of 2,937 plasma proteins, researchers found 446 dysregulated proteins in incident Parkinson cases and used machine learning to select a 23-protein panel for prediction.
  • Still unknown: The result is a retrospective biomarker/prediction study, not a validated screening test or evidence that intervention based on the panel improves outcomes. The external PPMI analysis retrained and tested models in that cohort rather than evaluating a frozen UK Biobank model; validation AUCs varied by visit definition, and the reported maximum was 0.76. Protein associations and co-expression modules do not establish causal mechanisms. It is distinct from the earlier 2024 iRBD study in this ledger (DOI 10.1038/s41467-024-48961-3): separate cohorts and a different 23-protein/14-year result versus an eight-protein targeted panel and up-to-seven-year conversion finding; this record does not claim first discovery of presymptomatic plasma signals in Parkinson disease.
  • AI role: Machine-learning classifiers were trained on UK Biobank plasma proteomic measurements to predict incident Parkinson disease; recursive feature elimination selected a 23-protein subset. The authors then tested the shared protein subset in the separate PPMI cohort using its own train/test split.

6 Aug 2025Institute for Diabetes Research and Metabolic Diseases, Helmholtz Munich/University of Tübingen; German Center for Diabetes Research; German Institute of Human Nutrition Potsdam-Rehbruecke; University Hospital Ulm; University of Lübeck; University of Potsdam

Blood DNA methylation machine learning signatures classified brain insulin resistance across three cohorts

A machine-learning framework applied to blood DNA-methylation profiles identified 540 CpG sites that classified brain insulin resistance in adults without type 2 diabetes. In the 167-person discovery cohort, the selected methylation signature was tested in two separate replication cohorts of 33 and 24 participants, with reported classification accuracy of 83–94%. The CpGs mapped to 445 genes enriched for neuronal-development and axonogenesis annotations; 98 sites showed significant blood–brain methylation correlation.

Technology: Supervised machine-learning framework using blood DNA-methylation profiles; a multi-fold elastic-net approach was described in the associated institutional and conference materials

Relevance 53 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

Result, AI contribution and limits

Evidence context (descriptions follow the cited sources; test type is a catalog classification):

  • Publication status: Peer-reviewed paper
  • Test type: retrospective or benchmark
  • Tested: In the 167-person discovery cohort, the selected methylation signature was tested in two separate replication cohorts of 33 and 24 participants, with reported classification accuracy of 83–94%.
  • Still unknown: This is a biomarker-classification study, not a prospective clinical screening or intervention study. The discovery cohort had 167 participants and the replication cohorts were small (n=33 and n=24); replication accuracy is reported as 83–94%, and larger independent cohorts are needed to establish transportability. Blood–brain methylation correlations at 98 sites support a proxy relationship but do not show that peripheral methylation causes brain insulin resistance. The authors describe potential future diagnostic use rather than demonstrated clinical utility.
  • AI role: The supervised model selected a 540-CpG methylation signature from peripheral blood measurements to classify participants with and without brain insulin resistance, and the signature was assessed in two replication cohorts. The model-derived CpG set was then used for differential-methylation, gene-annotation and blood–brain correlation analyses.

EHR deep learning and sequencing identify two previously undiagnosed Noonan syndrome cases

Investigators applied a deep-learning model to diagnosis text in the electronic health records of 92,428 pediatric patients. It flagged 171 patients above a prespecified Noonan syndrome risk threshold for chart review; genetic sequencing and specialist assessment identified two previously undiagnosed Noonan syndrome cases among evaluated patients, in addition to three patients diagnosed during the study period. The confirmed cases had pathogenic variants in Noonan-associated genes, including PTPN11 and LZTR1. This supplies real-world evidence that EHR-based model screening can surface rare-disease cases for clinical genetic evaluation.

Technology: Deep convolutional neural network trained on structured electronic-health-record diagnosis text to estimate Noonan syndrome risk

Deep learning mines venom proteomes for antimicrobial peptides active in vitro and in a mouse infection model

The APEX deep-learning model screened 16,123 venom proteins by generating and scoring 40,626,260 venom-encrypted peptides. After activity prediction and filtering for low similarity to known antimicrobial peptides, the authors selected 58 for experiments; 53 showed antimicrobial activity against at least one tested pathogen. Three selected peptides reduced bacterial counts after topical treatment in a mouse Acinetobacter baumannii skin-abscess model; the wolf-spider-derived Arachnoserver-5 peptide produced a reported three-log reduction versus untreated controls through day four, without significant body-weight change under the study conditions.

  • Tested: After activity prediction and filtering for low similarity to known antimicrobial peptides, the authors selected 58 for experiments; 53 showed antimicrobial activity against at least one tested pathogen.
  • Still unknown: Only 58 of the 386 low-similarity candidates were experimentally tested, and activity was measured against a defined panel of 11 strains; some tested peptides were cytotoxic. The paper notes possible ion-channel activity for many candidates and calls for follow-up safety testing. The authors filtered predicted hits for sequence dissimilarity to known antimicrobial peptides, synthesized a selected subset, and experimentally tested antimicrobial activity, cytotoxicity and selected animal-model efficacy. The AI model narrowed an otherwise very large peptide search space; assays established which selected candidates were active.

Prospective silent-trial validation of a fine-tuned pathology foundation model for EGFR mutation screening in lung adenocarcinoma

A fine-tuned Prov-GigaPath ViT-g model, named EAGLE, predicted EGFR mutation status from routine H&E slides plus clinical features in lung adenocarcinoma. Across an international dataset of 8,461 slides it achieved mean AUC 0.847 internally and 0.870 in external cohorts. In a four-month prospective silent trial on 197 primary lung-adenocarcinoma samples, EAGLE achieved AUC 0.890. Simulated AI-assisted triage thresholds reduced rapid molecular EGFR tests by up to 43% while maintaining the study’s performance criteria.

Relevance 60 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Result, AI contribution and limits

Evidence context (descriptions follow the cited sources; test type is a catalog classification):

  • Test type: prospective or independent check
  • Tested: Across an international dataset of 8,461 slides it achieved mean AUC 0.847 internally and 0.870 in external cohorts.
  • Still unknown: The four-month prospective trial was silent: AI outputs did not guide care or replace standard testing. The 43% reduction is a simulated triage workflow at a selected score threshold, not an observed reduction in tests or evidence of improved outcomes. The cohort was 197 primary cases at one real-time deployment site, while broader retrospective/external cohorts supported generalization. EAGLE predicts presence of EGFR mutation but does not identify the mutation subtype; sequencing remains necessary before treatment. Performance was lower on metastatic samples. The paper is a distinct 2025 model iteration and validation study in the lineage of the group’s 2022 arXiv proof of concept (10.48550/arXiv.2206.10573); the prior work is cited as antecedent, not treated as a second alias or hidden as the first-ever pathology-image EGFR result.
  • AI role: The AI model predicted tumor EGFR mutation status directly from routine H&E digital slides, using sequencing results as ground truth. Fine-tuning the pathology foundation model produced cross-institution validation, and real-time inference in a prospective silent trial tested generalization on newly processed clinical slides. The model score was evaluated as a screening/triage layer alongside rapid molecular testing; it did not replace genomic sequencing.

Instantaneous voice-synthesis neuroprosthesis for a man with ALS

A brain-computer interface decoding 256 microelectrodes in the ventral precentral gyrus synthesized the participant's intended voice causally, with a reported latency of about 10 ms per decoding step. 21 Feb 2025Skåne University Hospital; Lund University; Artera Inc.; University of California, San Francisco

Prospective Swedish cohort validates multimodal AI prostate-biopsy biomarker for recurrence and adverse pathology after prostatectomy

A previously developed multimodal AI score was retrospectively applied to archived diagnostic biopsies and follow-up from a prospectively collected Swedish prostatectomy cohort. The score, derived from digitized diagnostic prostate-biopsy images plus age, PSA and clinical T-stage, was associated with post-surgical biochemical recurrence and adverse pathology. Among 143 men with evaluable data and median 8.8-year follow-up, the continuous score was associated with recurrence (subdistribution HR 2.45, 95% CI 1.77–3.38); among 88 evaluable for adverse pathology, OR was 4.85 (95% CI 2.54–10.78). Estimated 5-year recurrence was 25% in intermediate/high score versus 4% in low score.

Technology: Artera multimodal artificial-intelligence (MMAI) prostate biomarker combining deep-learning features from digitized biopsy histopathology with age, PSA and clinical T-stage

  • Tested: For ex-vivo validation, the investigators sequenced tumor cells from seven patients with pancreatic or esophageal cancer and tested CHANCE-prioritized drugs; at least one predicted non-oncology drug showed anticancer activity in tumor cells from five of the seven patients.
  • Still unknown: Only seven patient-derived samples were tested, from pancreatic or esophageal cancers; at least one prioritized non-oncology drug showed activity in five. This was an ex-vivo drug-sensitivity assay, not clinical treatment, and the study does not establish efficacy, safety, dosing or patient benefit. Drug-response predictions may include drugs represented in training, as the article notes 149 of 923 screened drugs were in the training data.
  • AI role: Trained on drug-sensitivity measurements from 318 cancer cell lines across 647 drugs, CHANCE maps each patient tumor’s whole-genome mutations to drug-target/pathway features and ranks non-oncology drugs by predicted patient-specific anticancer activity. Investigators used these predictions to select drugs for ex-vivo testing in tumor cells from seven patients; the reported five-patient activity result tests the model’s personalized prioritization.

Eight proteins (VCAM1, LDHB, MSN, FLG2, TAGLN2, LMNA, MBL2 and LBP) showed consistency in an independent cohort of 183 patients and were confirmed by targeted parallel-reaction-monitoring mass spectrometry. The protein model AUC was 0.802 in validation versus 0.738 for the clinical model. The discovery analysis also reported sphingosine-1-phosphate association with ARDS prognosis and an enriched sphingolipid pathway.

Technology: LASSO and Boruta feature selection; machine-learning prognostic model; targeted PRM validation

Machine learning prioritizes 1-methylnicotinamide as a serum signal across HBV cirrhosis-to-HCC progression

Untargeted serum metabolomics from 69 participants, including eight patients followed from HBV-related cirrhosis to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), was analyzed with LASSO and random forest to prioritize metabolites. 1-methylnicotinamide (1-MNAM) declined across healthy, cirrhosis and HCC groups and was lower at the HCC than cirrhosis stage in the eight progressors. Targeted mass spectrometry in a separate cohort of 25 healthy controls and 25 early-stage HCC patients confirmed lower 1-MNAM in HCC (AUC 0.954 for HCC versus healthy controls).

1 Jun 2024Janssen Research & Development, LLC (Johnson & Johnson)

Deep learning on routine pathology slides prescreens FGFR-altered bladder cancers in a global study

A deep-learning device analyzed routine H&E whole-slide images to estimate whether advanced urothelial tumors carried selected FGFR2/FGFR3 alterations used for erdafitinib eligibility. In a separate 350-slide retrospective validation set, the device achieved 88.7% sensitivity and 31.8% specificity; it was also prospectively integrated into a non-interventional study spanning 89 sites in nine countries. The paper projected a 28.7% reduction in molecular tests assuming 15% biomarker prevalence; that estimate was simulated, not a measured population-level reduction.

Technology: FGFR Device, a multi-instance-learning attention model with a convolutional neural-network backbone

Relevance 60 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: prospective or independent check. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

Result, AI contribution and limits

Evidence context (descriptions follow the cited sources; test type is a catalog classification):

  • Publication status: Peer-reviewed paper
  • Test type: prospective or independent check
  • Tested: In a separate 350-slide retrospective validation set, the device achieved 88.7% sensitivity and 31.8% specificity; it was also prospectively integrated into a non-interventional study spanning 89 sites in nine countries.
  • Still unknown: The 350-slide retrospective validation set was deliberately enriched (150 FGFR-positive and 200 negative; 43% prevalence), and the device fell slightly short of the prespecified 90% sensitivity target. Prospective real-time workflow validation covered only 17 samples in one month (15 predictions; two quality-control failures); production deployment reported 24 samples, with only 20 receiving molecular testing. The 28.7% test reduction is a simulation assuming 15% prevalence, not an observed clinical outcome. This is prescreening support, not a stand-alone diagnosis or evidence of patient benefit.
  • AI role: Trained on more than 3,000 urothelial-cancer slides with molecular test labels, the deep-learning model inferred selected FGFR alteration status from H&E images and returned a likelihood for prescreening before confirmatory molecular testing. The device was prospectively integrated into a non-interventional study workflow; molecular tests remained the reference standard.

Evidence sources: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-49153-9.pdf

Both outcomes shared diabetes duration, insulin use, age and tyrosine as important model features. DKD additionally selected cardiovascular disease history, antihypertensive use, lactate, citrate and the intermediate-density-lipoprotein cholesterol-ester/total-lipid ratio; DR additionally selected HbA1c, glucose, pulse pressure and alanine. Relevance 53 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Result, AI contribution and limits

Evidence context (descriptions follow the cited sources; test type is a catalog classification):

  • Publication status: Peer-reviewed paper
  • Test type: retrospective or benchmark
  • Tested: In 2,772 adults with diabetes from Singapore’s population-based SEED study, LASSO and gradient-boosting models screened 220 circulating metabolites and 19 clinical factors for prevalent diabetic kidney disease (DKD) and retinopathy (DR), then were externally assessed in 5,843 UK Biobank participants.
  • Still unknown: The analysis is retrospective and cross-sectional; it classifies prevalent complications and cannot establish temporal prediction or causal effects of tyrosine, lactate, citrate, alanine or lipid features. The Singapore cohort was recruited in 2004–2011 and was multiethnic Asian; about 95% had type 2 diabetes, but the study did not separate diabetes types. UK Biobank definitions and available eye-severity measures differed, and validation of moderate-or-worse DR was not feasible. Performance is modest, particularly external AUC 0.791 DKD/0.778 DR, and does not establish clinical utility.
  • AI role: ML feature selection prioritized a shared set of clinical/metabolic factors and distinct DKD- and DR-associated metabolites, then built detection models externally evaluated in UK Biobank. These models outperformed traditional adjusted logistic-regression comparators in the reported internal and external validation. The scientific result is the disease-specific feature pattern and its validated detection performance, not merely an algorithm benchmark.

In an independent validation set, the panel distinguished hepatocellular carcinoma from cirrhosis (AUC 0.979; sensitivity 0.925; specificity 0.915) and from healthy controls (AUC 0.992). In a prospective external cohort of cirrhosis patients followed for HCC, it predicted conversion with AUC 0.890 and median lead time of 11.4 months before imaging diagnosis.

Technology: Random-forest machine-learning model for serum-protein panel selection and HCC classification

  • Tested: In an independent validation set, the panel distinguished hepatocellular carcinoma from cirrhosis (AUC 0.979; sensitivity 0.925; specificity 0.915) and from healthy controls (AUC 0.992). The prospectively collected cirrhosis cohort was split into 177 training and 76 validation participants for predictive-model construction; collection timing alone does not establish a prospective locked-model evaluation.
  • Still unknown: The prospective cohort included 253 cirrhosis patients, with 36 developing HCC; 8 of 65 participants were false positives for conversion by the reported endpoint. Deep learning detects elevated tissue-derived cfDNA across cancer and cirrhosis cohorts

Applying cfSort to patient data, the investigators found higher cfDNA fractions from the affected tissue in liver, lung, colorectal and stomach cancer and cirrhosis cohorts than in healthy controls; the estimated fractions also increased with cancer stage. Longitudinal EHR machine learning identifies patients who may need autoimmune rheumatic-disease evaluation years earlier

A random-forest model trained on longitudinal electronic health records from 161,584 people across two institutions identified records associated with high-specificity autoantibody testing for systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs). The model achieved AUROC 0.93 in internal validation and 0.87 on the external All of Us cohort. In a separate BioMe cohort, model probabilities tracked SARD and other autoimmune diagnoses; records could predict later autoantibody testing and rheumatology encounters up to five years before those events. The study also found higher autoantibody yield among model-prioritized individuals than under the comparison clinical-testing rate.

27 Jan 2023Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health; Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study centers; National University of Singapore; New York University Grossman School of Medicine; collaborating institutions

Elastic-net proteomic risk modeling and multi-cohort validation identify proteins associated with incident diabetes

An untargeted analysis of 4,955 plasma proteins in the ARIC cohort identified 140 associations with incident diabetes; 64 were significant in an internal sample and 47 (including 22 reported as novel) were associated in the external Singapore Multi-Ethnic Cohort. Elastic-net Cox modeling selected a 27-protein panel for 20-year risk prediction. In internal validation, adding those proteins to conventional risk factors including fasting glucose and HbA1c increased the C statistic from 0.720 to 0.731. Genetic-instrument analyses supported possible causal roles for SHBG, ATP1B2 and GSTA1, although ATP1B2’s genetic and observational directions differed.

Technology: Elastic-net Cox regression for protein feature selection and incident-diabetes risk prediction

  • Still unknown: The 47-protein associations were externally tested in Singapore MEC; the elastic-net predictive model itself was internally validated in ARIC, not independently externally validated. The causal claims are genetic-instrument inferences, not experimental proof; ATP1B2 had opposite directions in genetic-instrument versus observational analyses. Cohort associations do not establish clinical utility.
  • AI role: Elastic net selected a 27-protein combination from candidate proteins to improve 20-year incident-diabetes risk prediction beyond clinical and cardiometabolic covariates. The model was trained in the ARIC discovery subset and internally evaluated in a held-out ARIC subset. Separate Cox association and genetic-instrument analyses reported the externally validated protein associations; the record does not attribute those analyses to machine learning.

21 Jan 2023Stanford Health Care; Yale University; California Department of Public Health

Random-forest metabolite profiling reduces false-positive newborn screens for four inherited disorders

A 121-analyte LC–MS/MS panel combined established markers, untargeted-metabolomics features and chromatographically resolved isobars with random-forest classification of California newborn-screen dried blood spots. In 883 archived infant samples, the study reports that the second-tier approach maintained 100% sensitivity while reducing false positives by 83% for glutaric acidemia type I, 84% for methylmalonic acidemia, 100% for ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency and 51% for very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. Relevance 47 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Result, AI contribution and limits

  • Still unknown: This was a proof-of-principle second-tier simulation on residual archived California newborn-screen specimens, not a prospective implementation study. The validation sample was not a fully independent external set, and archived-sample degradation and processing batch effects limited biomarker discovery; some discriminating isobar identities and biological significance remain unknown. The reported sensitivity and false-positive reductions are cohort-specific and do not establish improved health outcomes or routine clinical utility.
  • AI role: The classifier modeled multianalyte profiles from true-positive and false-positive screen-positive samples to distinguish the groups for four inherited metabolic disorders. Feature-importance analysis showed that complex profiles, including unresolved long-chain acylcarnitine/hydroxy-acylcarnitine isobars, contributed to classification; the model's second-tier performance was assessed against known case status.

LSTM-designed peptides show antibacterial activity and mixed efficacy in a mouse sepsis model

8 Jun 2021University of California, San Francisco; Oregon Health & Science University

Cross-tissue machine learning prioritizes a 13-gene rheumatoid-arthritis activity score

A machine-learning feature-selection pipeline integrated public whole-blood (1,885 samples) and synovial-tissue (284 samples) transcriptomic datasets and selected a 13-gene rheumatoid-arthritis score. Across five independent transcriptomic datasets, the score tracked DAS28 disease activity, distinguished rheumatoid arthritis from osteoarthritis, separated polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis from healthy controls, and was associated with treatment effects. In an independent immunoblot cohort, two of six tested proteins, TNFAIP6/TSG-6 and HSP90AB1/HSP90, were confirmed.

Technology: Cross-tissue machine-learning feature-selection pipeline for transcriptomic data

Result, AI contribution and limits

Evidence context (descriptions follow the cited sources; test type is a catalog classification):

  • Publication status: Peer-reviewed paper
  • Test type: retrospective or benchmark
  • Tested: In an independent immunoblot cohort, two of six tested proteins, TNFAIP6/TSG-6 and HSP90AB1/HSP90, were confirmed.
  • Still unknown: The transcriptomic inputs were previously published datasets and the reported clinical associations are observational; the study does not establish a deployable diagnostic test or causal disease mechanism. Treatment-effect association should not be interpreted as prospective prediction of individual response.
  • AI role: The pipeline selected a compact 13-gene signature from public blood and synovial expression datasets; the study evaluated its association with disease activity and diagnostic distinctions across five independent transcriptomic datasets, then tested six selected proteins by immunoblot in a separate patient cohort.

A CNN trained on contrast-enhanced CT from a Taiwanese centre reached 98.3% sensitivity on combined local test sets versus 92.9% for radiologists (difference 5.4 points, p=0.014). On a US external test set, sensitivity fell to 79.0% with specificity 97.6% (AUC 0.920), and sensitivity for tumours under 2 cm was 63.1% in that set. The study is retrospective and the authors describe it as supplementary to radiologists.

Technology: Convolutional neural network applied to CT image patches

  • Tested: Multicenter prospective clinical trial (n = 278): CNN diagnosis of stimulated Raman images was non-inferior to pathologists reading conventional histology (94.6% versus 93.9%), in under 150 seconds.
  • Still unknown: Long-term patient outcomes are not reported in the abstract.
  • AI role: Convolutional neural networks trained on over 2.5 million stimulated Raman histology images.

Evidence sources: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-019-0715-9

1 Jan 2020Google DeepMind; Google Health, Cancer Research UK Imperial Centre, and Northwestern University

An AI breast-cancer screening system evaluated in two countries

Among 25,856 women in the UK and 3,097 in the US, the system reduced false positives by 5.7% (US) and 1.2% (UK), and false negatives by 9.4% and 2.7% in absolute terms compared with radiologists. Trained only on UK data, it also outperformed specialists on US data. Retrospective evaluation (Nature): prospective studies are needed, and clinical deployment is unclear.

Technology: Neural network for mammograms

Relevance 60 medicine Original sourcePaper Suggest a correction

Publication: Peer-reviewed paper · Test context: retrospective or benchmark. Catalog categories, not an evidence grade.

Result, AI contribution and limits

Evidence context (descriptions follow the cited sources; test type is a catalog classification):

  • Publication status: Peer-reviewed paper
  • Test type: retrospective or benchmark
  • Tested: Retrospective evaluation on UK (25,856 women) and US (3,097 women) screening mammograms, compared with individual radiologists' decisions; a reader study and a simulated double-reading workflow were also run.
  • Still unknown: The authors state prospective studies are required and that how to deploy the system clinically is not yet determined; the US data were enriched; the second-reader scenario was only simulated.
  • AI role: Predicted from screening mammograms alone whether a biopsy would later show cancer.

Evidence sources: https://deepmind.google/blog/international-evaluation-of-an-ai-system-for-breast-cancer-screening/ · https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=DOI:10.1038/s41586-019-1799-6&resultType=core&format=json
